title: Stained glass
hookLine: windows as a Bible for people who couldn't read

cards: What does a woman who can't read see when she walks into a medieval church on a bright morning? Not words. Color.
A blue so deep it looks like night, a red like a coal in the hearth. And inside the color, people: a man asleep under a ladder of angels, a woman at a well, a baby in a manger, a body on a cross.
As the sun moves, one window brightens, then the next, and the stories light up in turn. She can't read a page, but she can read the wall.

teach.h: PICTURES FOR THOSE WHO CAN'T READ.
teach.b: First, the reason for pictures. Pope Gregory the Great once wrote to a bishop who had smashed the images in his church, worried that people were worshiping them.
Gregory told him he was right to forbid worship of images, and wrong to break them.

What writing gives to those who can read, he said, a picture gives to the unlearned who look at it: in it they read what they cannot read in books. That's why the windows get called a Bible for people who couldn't read.

teach.h: A STORY TOLD PANEL BY PANEL.
teach.b: Second, the way the story is told. A window is cut into panels, scene after scene, like a comic strip, so a life can be followed picture by picture. Third, the light itself.

teach.h: THE TRUE LIGHT, GIVEN BACK IN COLOR.
teach.b: John's Gospel says of Christ, in the Douay-Rheims: "That was the true light, which enlighteneth every man that cometh into this world." Glass makes no light of its own.
It receives the sun and gives it back in color, shaped into a story.

Suger, a medieval abbot who rebuilt the abbey church of Saint-Denis near Paris, wrote that beauty seen with the eyes could lead the mind up toward that true light. Finally, the thing that's easy to forget.

teach.h: DARK UNTIL THE SUN COMES THROUGH.
teach.b: From inside the church at night, a stained-glass window is dark. The lead lines are there, the colors are there, but the story waits.
It only speaks when light comes through.

how: Catholic churches old and new use stained-glass windows to show scenes from scripture and the lives of the saints, and some parishes offer tours or guides that walk visitors through the stories window by window.

o: glass painted to keep sunlight out of a church
glass darkened by age and candle smoke
colored glass in lead, telling stories in pictures

p: pictures are books for the unlearned
a story told scene by scene

s: Gregory the Great praised a bishop for smashing church images
he told him not to let people worship images, and not to break them either: pictures teach those who can't read.
seen from inside at night, a stained-glass window goes dark
the glass makes no light of its own. the story only shows when light comes through.
stained glass was only ever decoration
it was meant to be read: scripture and the saints' lives, told panel by panel.

games.q: you're a bishop. people in your town have started worshiping the pictures on your church walls. what do you do?
o: smash the pictures so no one can worship them.
keep the pictures and teach what they're for.
cover them up and say nothing.
games.why: a bishop who smashed his images was told by Gregory the Great to forbid the worship, and keep the pictures as books for the unlearned.

practice: Find light passing through glass: a window, a glass of water, a jar held up to a lamp. Watch how the glass bends the light, colors it, throws it onto the table, while doing nothing on its own.
If you pray, hold John's line, the true light, which enlighteneth every man; if not, let the light be the only thing happening for a while.

wordCard.voice: Stained glass. Colored glass set in lead, cut into panels that tell scripture and the saints' lives to anyone who can see, whether or not they can read. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: light that tells stories. A window can be a page, if you know how to read it. That's day eight hundred eighteen.
